query: FeNiCrCoCu is considered suitable for thin-film use, and its expense favors applying it as a protective coating on conventional metals rather than using it in bulk. Earlier studies examined room-temperature wear behavior in relation to coating–substrate combinations, composition, and grain size, but largely addressed the alloy itself or a limited thermal regime rather than the overall wear response of a coating across different temperatures. Under the constraints that FeNiCrCoCu remains a thin protective coating and that high-temperature wear is the target application, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs its overall wear resistance and why? Specify an intervention relative to a baseline coating condition, predict the observations expected if the hypothesis is correct, state the applicable temperature and loading boundaries, connect the hypothesis to prior evidence, and identify a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: A pre-oxidation heat treatment that forms a uniform, continuous, copper-enriched oxide (or spinel) glaze on the as-deposited thin-film FeNiCrCoCu coating will improve its high-temperature wear resistance by acting as a protective barrier during sliding contact.
generation.material_initial_state: As-deposited FeNiCrCoCu thin-film coating on a conventional metal substrate, with its native microstructure and without a pre-formed oxide layer.
generation.intervention: Apply a controlled pre-oxidation heat treatment (e.g., at a temperature and duration optimized to promote copper segregation and continuous oxide formation) prior to wear testing.
generation.conditions: High-temperature sliding wear tests conducted at temperatures between 400°C and 600°C under controlled load conditions representative of service environments for protective coatings.
generation.structural_mediator: The continuous, adherent copper-enriched oxide (or spinel-rich) glaze that forms on the coating’s surface during pre-oxidation.
generation.mechanism: The pre-formed oxide glaze reduces direct metal-to-metal contact and limits further oxidation, thereby decreasing friction and mechanical wear. Copper segregation within the oxide may enhance the glaze’s integrity and adhesion under sliding loads.
generation.predicted_outcome: When compared to the as-deposited baseline, the pre-oxidized coating will show lower coefficients of friction, reduced wear track depth, and lower overall mass loss during high-temperature sliding tests.
generation.baseline: As-deposited thin-film FeNiCrCoCu coatings tested under the same high-temperature wear conditions without pre-oxidation treatment.
generation.boundary: Results are expected to hold within the defined testing regime (400–600°C, typical sliding contact loads). At significantly higher temperatures or under extreme loads, the oxide layer may degrade, and the mechanism may not be effective.
generation.uncertainty: The exact degree of copper enrichment, oxide continuity, and their stability under variable thermal and mechanical conditions need further quantification. Optimization of pre-oxidation parameters is required to ensure consistent oxide formation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two groups of FeNiCrCoCu thin-film coatings on an identical metal substrate: one group remains as-deposited (baseline) and the other undergoes the controlled pre-oxidation heat treatment. Subject both groups to identical high-temperature sliding wear tests (e.g., ball-on-disk tests) at temperatures between 400°C and 600°C under a prescribed load and sliding speed. Prior to and after the wear tests, characterize the surface oxide morphology and composition using SEM and EDS.
measurements: Coefficient of friction during wear tests
Wear track depth and volume loss (from profilometry)
Continuity and composition of the oxide glaze (via SEM/EDS)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the pre-oxidized coatings do not exhibit significantly lower friction, reduced wear track depth, and lower mass loss compared to the as-deposited coatings under identical test conditions, then the hypothesis that the copper-enriched oxide glaze is the key factor governing improved high-temperature wear resistance will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract In this paper, the Si-20Cr-20Fe coating was prepared on MoNbTaTiW RHEA by a fused slurry method. The microstructural evolution and compositions of the silicide coating under high-temperature oxidation environment were studied. The results show that the silicide coating could effectively prevent the oxidation of the MoNbTaTiW RHEA. The initial silicide coating had a double-layer structure: a high silicon content layer mainly composed of MSi 2 as the outer layer and a low silicon content layer mainly contained M 5 Si 3 as the inner layer. Under high-temperature oxidation conditions, the silicon element diffused from the silicide coating to the RHEA substrate while the oxidation of the coating occurred. After oxidation, the coating was composed of an outer oxide layer and an inner silicide layer. The silicide layer moved toward the inside of the substrate, led to the increase of its thickness. Compared with the initial silicified layer, its structure did not change significantly. The structure and compositions of the oxide layer on the outer surface strongly depended on the oxidation temperature. High-entropy alloys (HEAs) present a new approach of alloying concepts. Whereas conventional alloys usually comprise one major alloying element and minor additions of other alloying elements to improve properties, HEAs consist of at least five elements with close to equimolar composition. For several compositions, the desired formation of solely solid solutions with a face-centred cubic (fcc) or a body-centred cubic (bcc) structure could be achieved [ [1] , [2] , [3] ].

Several groups of HEAs have been intensively investigated. The term compositionally complex alloys (CCAs) was introduced for HEAs with a multiphase microstructure [ [4] ]. Several investigations prove the formation of primarily cubic phases in the alloy AlCoCrCuFeNi and its derivatives [ [5] , [6] , [7] ]. Aluminium strongly influences the microstructure, phase formation and resulting properties. Furthermore, aluminium acts as a stabiliser of bcc solid solutions and can suppress the formation of complex phases [ [8] , [9] , [10] ]. decision.trend: Early investigations into high-entropy alloy (HEA) coatings have mostly focused on individual factors – such as composition, grain size or coating–substrate interactions – at room temperature, or on isolated mechanical phenomena, rather than the integrated overall wear behavior across an extended thermal regime. In one study (PMC7515071), elevated temperature reciprocating wear tests on an AlCoCrFeNiTi0.5 HEA revealed that wear resistance improves at high temperatures due to the in situ formation of protective oxide (spinel) phases. This work, along with others examining microstructural evolution and oxidation behavior, indicates that thermally activated surface oxidation may be a key player in controlling wear resistance. However, despite these insights, there remains a gap regarding how a thermally evolved oxide glaze (potentially with selective elemental segregation) governs the macroscopic wear response in thin-film HEA coatings like FeNiCrCoCu under service-like, high-temperature conditions.
decision.unsolved: It remains undetermined whether and how the controlled formation of a continuous, adherent, and compositionally optimized oxide layer (likely influenced by the copper content) on a thin FeNiCrCoCu coating can act as a mechanistic barrier to wear at high temperature. In particular, the interplay between oxidation kinetics, oxide scale adherence, and the coating–substrate interface under elevated temperature sliding contact has not been systematically quantified.
decision.lever: Introduce a pre-oxidation heat treatment (relative to an as-deposited baseline) to induce the formation of a continuous, copper-enriched oxide (or spinel)-rich glaze, then perform high-temperature (e.g., 400–600°C) sliding wear tests under controlled load.
decision.why: This step directly builds on the trend observed in prior studies where high-temperature exposure promotes the formation of protective oxides that improve wear resistance. By deliberately pre-forming such an oxide layer via controlled thermal activation, the experiment isolates the effect of the oxide’s evolution on overall wear performance, thereby testing the hypothesis that the integrity and composition of the thermally induced glaze (with Cu segregation playing a key role) primarily govern the high-temperature wear resistance of a thin-film FeNiCrCoCu coating. A falsification of the hypothesis would occur if the controlled oxide formation does not reduce friction/wear or if the oxide layer fails under high mechanical load, implying that other mechanisms are responsible for the wear behavior.

families.best_lever: Design an experiment that modifies the coating (e.g., by controlled heat treatment or interfacial alloying) to influence diffusion or oxide formation, and concurrently perform simulations that predict how such changes regulate wear resistance at 400–600°C under specified mechanical loads. Observing a mismatch between predicted and actual wear would then falsify the hypothesis.
